As vibecoding—AI-prompt-assisted programming—becomes increasingly popular, the number of newly listed apps on the App Store has surged, doubling in the first half of 2026, but downloads only grew by 2%. Details below.

New App Store listings soar, but downloads fail to keep pace

A report published today by The New York Times cites the latest data from Sensor Tower, noting that the number of newly listed apps on the App Store doubled in the first half of 2026, while downloads rose only modestly by 2%:

The Times report also profiles two developers who have launched apps on the App Store through vibecoding—Marco Pérez, who plans to leave his job at JPMorgan next month to work on app development full-time, and David Svensson, who has released 11 niche apps over the past five months and treats vibecoding more as a hobby than a business opportunity.

The report reads as follows:

Pérez, a software engineer based in Chicago, had never built a mobile app before. He spent five weeks over the winter tinkering with 'vibecoding' AI tools to build a prototype, followed by another two weeks preparing the app for release on the App Store. The app, called InfoDrizzle, has performed reasonably well so far, recording 1,300 downloads and earning about $500. Pérez's next app proved even more popular. In May, he built and launched Stampa—a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps—in roughly just one week. Stampa has since racked up 20,000 downloads and earned around $3,000.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian addressed another consequence of this listing surge when responding to The New York Times: earlier reports had suggested the App Store review process has come under pressure as a result.

Ajemian said that 'Apple has consistently been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours,' and added that Apple is 'delighted to see a new generation of developers harnessing the latest tools to build and launch apps at unprecedented speed.'

He also stressed that 'all apps are held to the same high standards of quality, privacy, and safety that users have come to trust,' regardless of whether they were built using vibecoding.
